isolation_audit.comparison: Sec 5.3 (RQ3), Table 4: raw functions flagged by GPT matching before vs after static confirmation, on Web3Bugs
isolation_audit.model_config: Same run of the same pipeline, so the same model in both arms. Sec 4.5 names GPT-3.5-turbo; Sec 5.3 names no model.
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: Web3Bugs only; counts of raw (unmerged) candidate functions, 647 before vs 221 after
isolation_audit.budget_control: not applicable; GPT input is identical in both arms (the arms are two stages of one run)
isolation_audit.arm_a: GPT-matched candidate functions (pure GPT-based matching output)
isolation_audit.arm_b: Same candidates after the static-analysis (dataflow) confirmation stage filters them
isolation_audit.other_changes: Adds or removes the static confirmation stage, a symbolic post-filter. GPT's input representation does not change. It is a before/after measurement within one run, not a separately run ablation.
isolation_audit.delta: "Static confirmation effectively filtered out 65.84% of the false positive cases in the Web3Bugs dataset" (647 -> 221 raw functions); "only 3 ground-truth cases were initially matched by GPT but later excluded by static analysis"
isolation_audit.rationale: RQ3 examines "how static confirmation reduces false positives generated by pure GPT-based matching." The varied factor is a symbolic confirmation stage, not the representation supplied to GPT. The paper contains no input-representation ablation: its only other comparisons use David et al.'s published GPT-only figures and a GPT-4 model swap. The 426 filtered raw functions include a few ground-truth cases, so 65.84% is a reduction in raw functions, not a clean false-positive count.

isolation_audit.comparison: Sec 5.2 (RQ2) Table 4, input-component ablation: VulMaster full vs '-w/o AST' ("excluding the AST traversals")
isolation_audit.model_config: Same in both arms: adapted-CodeT5 in the FiD framework, fine-tuned (Adam, batch 64, 20 epochs, max 10 segments x 512 tokens); the ablated variant is a model trained without AST segments (retraining procedure not separately described)
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: CVEFixes + Big-Vul merged C/C++ repair dataset (VulRepair split, deduplicated); Exact Match (Top-1)
isolation_audit.budget_control: Partial cap only: FiD max 10 segments of 512 tokens in both arms, but the AST arm adds AST node-sequence segments and the authors note ~90% of samples use fewer than 10 segments, so the cap rarely binds; the AST arm is longer. Not controlled
isolation_audit.arm_a: Full input: whole vulnerable function (segmented) + serialized AST node sequence (DFS traversal, segmented) + CWE knowledge (name, CWE examples, ChatGPT-generated fixes)
isolation_audit.arm_b: Same input without the AST node-sequence segments
isolation_audit.other_changes: none (same FiD architecture, relevance-prediction task and model adaptation; only the AST input segments are dropped, at training and inference)
isolation_audit.delta: Table 4: EM 20.0 (full) vs 19.0 (-w/o AST), i.e. -1.0 pp; text: "the complete function, structural information, and CWE knowledge bring 6%, 5%, and 5.5% improvements" (relative)
isolation_audit.rationale: Removing the AST only removes input segments from the same model ("(2) VulMaster w/o AST: excluding the AST traversals"), but the AST is added as extra segments on top of the full function, and the 10x512 segment cap is not binding for ~90% of samples, so the structured arm carries more context. Representation is confounded with input amount.
isolation_audit.human_reason: 10x512 segment cap rarely binds (~90% of samples below it), so the AST arm usually carries more input.

isolation_audit.comparison: RQ2 (Section VI-B), Tables III-V and VII-VIII: with context supplementation ('C') vs. without ('N'), within each model x knowledge (Nk/Ok/Sk) x prompt-scheme cell
isolation_audit.model_config: Same model within each cell (GPT-4.1, Phi-3-mini-128k, Llama-3-8B, o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B); provider-default config, temperature 0 (o4-mini excepted); identical knowledge prefix and prompt scheme in both arms
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: UniVul (Solidity, Java, C/C++; 147 vulnerable + 147 non-vulnerable); TP counts, precision, recall, F1 as annotated by GPT-4.1
isolation_audit.budget_control: not controlled / not reported; the C arm appends extra code (callees, plus report-mentioned related functions for vulnerable samples) to the same prompt, so it is longer
isolation_audit.arm_a: Target code + knowledge prefix + prompt scheme, plus static-analysis-extracted context: callees for all samples and related functions mentioned in the vulnerability report for vulnerable samples
isolation_audit.arm_b: Target code + the same knowledge prefix and prompt scheme, no supplementary context
isolation_audit.other_changes: none in the pipeline (context is 'processed before feeding the code into LLMs' via static analysis). Caveat: the report-derived related-function context exists only for vulnerable samples, so the added context is label-correlated
isolation_audit.delta: "For Solidity, 22 out of 36 model–prompt–knowledge combinations show an increase in TPs with context, while 11 show a decrease. In Java, 18 combinations show an increase and 15 a decrease. C/C++ ... 28 combinations showing increased TPs and only 7 showing a decrease." (counts of cells, not pp)
isolation_audit.rationale: Same model and prompt; only the supplied context differs ('we use static analysis to ensure the same contexts for the given code across all models'), but the context arm adds code and no length/token control is reported, so representation is confounded with context amount. The prior's 'same model/budget' claim is unsupported; additionally, report-mentioned related code is added only for vulnerable samples.

isolation_audit.comparison: §VII-C RQ3 ablation, Table IV: full ACFix vs 'W/o ACG' (token costs in Table VI, §VII-F)
isolation_audit.model_config: Same in both arms: GPT-4-0613 generator + validator (MAD), RBAC taxonomy, static grammar checks; temperature 0, max 4096 output tokens
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: 118-case AC vulnerability benchmark; repair success rate (fixed/118)
isolation_audit.budget_control: Not explicitly capped, but the structured arm is shorter: Table VI avg tokens ACFix 1,956.35 vs W/o ACG 2,813.68 ('W/o ACG consumed more tokens than ACFix because the raw source code was not processed')
isolation_audit.arm_a: Full ACFix: serialized AC Context Graph (interprocedural slice over PDG + call graph, with edges described in NL) supplied to GPT-4
isolation_audit.arm_b: W/o ACG: same pipeline, raw contract source code supplied in place of the ACG
isolation_audit.other_changes: none reported ('W/o ACG has the same implementation as ACFix but without ACG'); note 5 contracts exceeded the token limit in W/o ACG (patches generated for 113/118), counted as failures
isolation_audit.delta: 106 vs 112 of 118 fixed: 89.83% vs 94.92% (-5.09 pp); paper: 'ACG contributed to 12 more successful cases' (Answer to RQ3)
isolation_audit.rationale: 'W/o ACG has the same implementation as ACFix but without ACG', and W/o ACG instead incorporates 'the raw source code of contracts' in the prompt, so only the code context supplied to the same GPT-4 pipeline changes. The structured arm is shorter (Table VI: 1,956 vs 2,814 avg tokens). Caveat: up to 5 of the 6 lost cases may stem from token-limit overflow in the raw-code arm (113 vs 118 patches generated), so part of the gain is context-length feasibility rather than representation quality. Also, the paper's 'additional 12 cases' conflicts with its own Table IV (112-106 = 6).

isolation_audit.comparison: RQ4 Table 6: SCALE vs Without SCTC
isolation_audit.model_config: UniXcoder with SCT-enhanced representation and cross-attention
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: FFMPeg+Qemu, Reveal, SVulD (8:1:1 splits); F1 (also Acc/P/R)
isolation_audit.budget_control: Not reported; SCT adds structured natural-language context.
isolation_audit.arm_a: SCALE using SCT
isolation_audit.arm_b: Without SCTC using comment tree
isolation_audit.other_changes: None reported beyond SCT construction.
isolation_audit.delta: Removing SER drops F1 by "1.31, 3.61, and 3.56" points (Table 6: 65.11->63.80, 62.85->59.24, 26.94->23.38). Removing SCTC drops F1 by "1.29, 2.59, and 2.04" points; the paper's SVulD figure does not match Table 6 (26.94-24.99=1.95).
isolation_audit.rationale: The cited ablation removes SER, which "fuse[s] the representation of source code and structured natural language comment through Cross-Attention," an architectural component, and also removes source code from the input. The cleanest comparison is Without SCTC (plain comment tree vs SCT, same architecture), but its input lengths are not reported, so at best it is R-unmatched-budget, not R-strict. Table 3 and RQ2 swap backbones, so they are not isolated.
isolation_audit.human_reason: Judge the cleanest comparison (Without SCTC vs SCALE): same architecture, structured comment tree adds text, lengths unreported. The cited 'Without SER' arm removes an architecture module.

isolation_audit.comparison: Sec 5.4 (RQ4) Table 10: C1 SPVR (full prompt) vs C2 Without_MET_info
isolation_audit.model_config: Same in both arms: ChatGPT-3.5-turbo-0125, "same settings as RQ2"
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: CVEFixes C/C++ subset, 547 samples; Pass@3 (exact match to ground truth in any of 3 outputs) and CodeBLEU
isolation_audit.budget_control: Not controlled; the MET arm adds MET-derived repair instructions to a prompt that is otherwise identical, so it is longer
isolation_audit.arm_a: CWE-related information + MET-related (AST minimum-edit-tree derived) repair instructions + regenerated code
isolation_audit.arm_b: CWE-related information + regenerated code (MET-related information removed)

isolation_audit.delta: Table 10: Pass@3 138 vs 55 (of 547); CodeBLEU 0.4456 vs 0.2646; text: "The pass@3 rate decreases to 55/547, representing a loss of over 50% compared to the baseline"
isolation_audit.rationale: Same model and dataset, and C2 only "remove[s] the MET-related information from the prompt", but the structured arm is the baseline plus extra AST-derived instructions with no budget control, so structure is confounded with added guidance text (which is also directive repair advice, not just a representation).

isolation_audit.comparison: Table 4 (RQ3, Section 5.3): Multi-round SIFT (MSIVD-) vs. Multi-round SIFT + GNN (MSIVD) on BigVul
isolation_audit.model_config: Both arms start from the same multitask-fine-tuned CodeLlama-13B-Instruct, but the classifier differs: MSIVD- converts it to sequence classification 'using a single linear layer'; MSIVD trains a separate sequence-to-classification model (DeepDFA GGNN adapter, embeddings concatenated with LLM hidden states, model dim 4352, 11 layers, LR 1e-6, 5 epochs; Table 2). Training configuration of the MSIVD- head is not separately reported
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: BigVul; F1 (also precision/recall)
isolation_audit.budget_control: not applicable as a prompt budget; same 2048-token context window in both arms. Trainable parameters and training procedure differ
isolation_audit.arm_a: Fine-tuned LLM hidden states concatenated with GGNN embeddings learned over CFG-based dataflow (DFA) features
isolation_audit.arm_b: Fine-tuned LLM hidden states with a single linear classification layer
isolation_audit.other_changes: Architecture (added GNN adapter layers, larger model dimension), and a separate classification training loop with its own hyperparameters; the graph is not an input to the LLM but a jointly trained neural module
isolation_audit.delta: "the additional GNN (multi-round SIFT + GNN) provides an additional 0.02 F1 on top of multi-round SIFT for the BigVul dataset" (F1 0.90 -> 0.92, absolute)
isolation_audit.rationale: MSIVD- 'converts the first model into a sequence-to-classification model directly, using a single linear layer', whereas MSIVD adds GNN layers trained in a separate loop (Table 2: model dim 4352, 11 layers, LR 1e-6), so model architecture and training differ between arms, not just the representation supplied. No same-model input-only comparison exists in the paper.
isolation_audit.human_reason: Adding the graph adds a trained GNN adapter (model dimension 4096->4352, separate training loop); the graph is never LLM input.

isolation_audit.comparison: §5.1 RQ3, Table 4: Vul-RAG (knowledge-level RAG) vs code-level RAG baseline, per LLM
isolation_audit.model_config: Same LLM per row (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 3.5, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, DeepSeek); the knowledge base is built offline with GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 (Vul-RAG arm only)
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: PairVul (586 Linux-kernel vulnerable/patched pairs, top-10 CWEs); pair accuracy (also balanced recall/precision)
isolation_audit.budget_control: Not reported; no token accounting for either arm
isolation_audit.arm_a: Vul-RAG: top-10 LLM-extracted, abstracted knowledge items (functional semantics, causes, fixing solutions) retrieved by code + abstract purpose + detailed behavior queries (BM25 + RRF re-ranking), then checked iteratively one item per prompt
isolation_audit.arm_b: Code-level RAG: similar code snippets retrieved by code similarity from the training set and added to the prompt (Fig. 5(b))
isolation_audit.other_changes: Retrieval stage differs (LLM-generated semantic queries, three-query BM25 + RRF vs code-only retrieval, so different items are retrieved); inference paradigm differs (iterative per-knowledge-item checking with early stop vs single augmented prompt); an extra LLM (GPT-3.5) builds the knowledge base
isolation_audit.delta: Pair accuracy, code RAG -> Vul-RAG: GPT-4o 0.05->0.32, Claude 0.11->0.27, Qwen 0.09->0.26, DeepSeek 0.05->0.30 (+16 to +27 points absolute; Table 4)
isolation_audit.rationale: The authors attribute the gain to two sources: '(1) In the retrieval phase, knowledge-level RAG more accurately retrieves semantically relevant vulnerabilities ... (2) In the inference phase ... the high-level representation'. The retrieval stage and the iterative detection loop both change along with the representation. No same-retrieval comparison isolates the representation alone.

isolation_audit.comparison: Table I: repair with no knowledge (15%) vs repair with CWE detail (31%)
isolation_audit.model_config: GitHub Copilot; same 156 buffer-overflow snippets; manual repair-success metric
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: Custom set of 156 buffer-overflow C snippets; manually judged repair success rate
isolation_audit.budget_control: Not reported; the CWE-detail prompt adds context and is longer.
isolation_audit.arm_a: Repair prompt with no additional knowledge
isolation_audit.arm_b: Repair prompt with CWE details
isolation_audit.other_changes: None reported beyond prompt context.
isolation_audit.delta: 15% (24/156) no-context repair vs 63% after full context-aware prompt tuning (">4x")
isolation_audit.rationale: The 63% figure comes from a multi-stage process in which, "if detection is wrong, the author supplies the correct answer," and failed repairs escalate to the next stage. Interaction paradigm, human feedback, and retries therefore vary along with context. The cleaner single-prompt comparison, no context 15% vs CWE detail 31% (48/156), has the same model and only added context, but prompt length is not reported, so it would be R-unmatched-budget, not R-strict. The paper's text and Table I are also inconsistent on the disclosure and CWE percentages.
isolation_audit.human_reason: Judge the cleaner single-prompt comparison (no context 15% vs CWE detail 31%): same model, added context, length unreported. The cited 63% arm is interactive with human correction and retries.

isolation_audit.comparison: Sec IV-D1 (RQ3) Table III: LLM4FPM (eCPG-Slicer + FARF) vs LLM4FPM-noslice
isolation_audit.model_config: Same in both arms: qwen2.5-32b, locally deployed; ablations use "the same experimental configurations as those for LLM4FPM on this dataset"
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: Juliet (SAST warnings from Cppcheck/Infer/CSA, 7 CWEs; 7,194 warnings per arm); Accuracy and F1
isolation_audit.budget_control: Structured arm shorter: the slice is a subset of the FARF-identified files; the unsliced arm feeds complete files and overflows the context window on 40 cases
isolation_audit.arm_a: eCPG line-level slice over the FARF-identified dependent files + bug report
isolation_audit.arm_b: Complete content of the same FARF-identified files + bug report ("Instead of slicing the code, the complete content of the files identified by the FARF algorithm is directly fed to the LLM")
isolation_audit.other_changes: none (same FARF file selection, prompt and model); the 40 context-overflow cases in the noslice arm are counted as errors in Table III
isolation_audit.delta: Table III: Accuracy 98.17% vs 95.15% (+3.02 pp), F1 98.92% vs 97.19% (+1.73 pp); "LLM4FPM-noslice additionally fails on 40 test cases because the input files exceeded the LLM's context window limit"
isolation_audit.rationale: Same model, dataset and configuration; the only change is whether the FARF files are sliced or passed whole, and the sliced (structured) arm is the shorter one. Part of the gap comes from the 40 overflow failures of the longer arm, which favours the structured arm by budget rather than against it. (The -nofarf arm, by contrast, changes file retrieval and is a component ablation.)

isolation_audit.comparison: Table III (Section III-C): RAG + CoT vs. No RAG
isolation_audit.model_config: GPT-4o in both arms with the CoT prompt; other configuration (temperature etc.) not reported
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: Big-Vul balanced test set (5,000 instances, 1:1); accuracy, precision, recall, F1
isolation_audit.budget_control: not reported; the RAG arm adds a retrieved CWE/CVE record to the prompt, so it is longer
isolation_audit.arm_a: Code snippet + CoT prompt + one retrieved Big-Vul record (top-5 by OpenAI embedding similarity from a 500-instance ChromaDB store, then 'GPT-4o later examines these records and selects the best one')
isolation_audit.arm_b: Code snippet + CoT prompt, no retrieval
isolation_audit.other_changes: Retrieval stage removed: embedding lookup in a vector DB plus an extra GPT-4o selection step over the top-5 candidates
isolation_audit.delta: F1 33.49% (RAG + CoT) vs 23.92% (No RAG), i.e. 9.57 pp; accuracy 89.68% vs 76.42%
isolation_audit.rationale: The ablation removes 'the RAG component', which is a pipeline stage (vector DB retrieval plus a GPT-4o step that 'examines these records and selects the best one') that also changes what is shown. The added-context arm is longer, with no budget control. It is not a representation-only swap.

isolation_audit.comparison: §V-B RQ2, Table IV: CGP-Tuning vs 'CGP-Tuning w/o cross-modal alignment' (also checked: Table III, Prompt Tuning vs CGP-Tuning)
isolation_audit.model_config: Same frozen backbone in each pair (CodeLlama, CodeGemma, Qwen2.5-Coder, 7B); separately trained adapters with different architectures; same optimizer/LR/1 epoch, 32 soft prompt embeddings
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: DiverseVul (under-sampled); accuracy (also P/R/F1). The Table IV CGP-Tuning row (0.6627 CodeLlama) differs from Table III (0.6582), and the split used for Table IV is not stated
isolation_audit.budget_control: Soft-prompt budget fixed at 32 embeddings in both arms; text input identical; max 16,000 tokens at test
isolation_audit.arm_a: Full CGP-Tuning: CPG (Joern) -> type-aware + positional embeddings -> GAT -> multi-head cross-attention + projector -> 32 graph-enhanced soft prompts + code text
isolation_audit.arm_b: W/o cross-modal alignment: skips step 10 and 'uses the soft prompt embeddings at step 2 directly' (graph features no longer reach the LLM) + code text
isolation_audit.other_changes: Trained adapter architecture and parameter count differ (alignment module, i.e. attention + projector, removed); each arm is a separately trained model
isolation_audit.delta: Accuracy 0.6627->0.4752 (CodeLlama, -18.75 pp), 0.6154->0.4700 (CodeGemma, -14.54 pp), 0.6572->0.5123 (Qwen, -14.49 pp); paper: 'accuracy drops of approximately 19, 15, and 14 percentage points' (Table IV)
isolation_audit.rationale: The ablated arm is a different trained model: removing the alignment module changes the learned adapter's architecture, not just the input ('plain soft prompt embeddings cannot bridge the semantic gap ... without the multi-head attention mechanism, nor ... without the projection'). The closest representation contrast, Prompt Tuning vs CGP-Tuning in Table III (equal 32-embedding budget, same hyperparameters; accuracy 0.5901->0.6582 CodeLlama, 0.5113->0.6219 CodeGemma, 0.5758->0.6507 Qwen), also adds a trainable graph encoder, so it is not R-strict either. The arm without alignment (0.4752) also scores below plain Prompt Tuning (0.5901), which points to an optimization artifact rather than the value of the CPG.
isolation_audit.human_reason: The paper's ablation removes a trained alignment module (different trained model); the GRACE comparison is a different method.

isolation_audit.comparison: Table 6 / Appendix C ablations: RepoAudit vs RepoAudit-NoAbs and vs RepoAudit-NoVal
isolation_audit.model_config: Same agent and LLM in every arm. The ablation section names no model; Sec 4 says Claude 3.5 Sonnet powers RepoAudit.
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: 15-project C/C++ benchmark (NPD, MLK, UAF); TP/FP counts and precision
isolation_audit.budget_control: not reported (no token or cost figures for NoAbs or NoVal; cost is reported only for NoCache, Table 7)
isolation_audit.arm_a: Full RepoAudit: function code plus a three-step hint prompt (pointer handling, abstraction, path exploration), followed by the validator
isolation_audit.arm_b: NoAbs: the same code, minus the second (abstraction) step of the prompt template. NoVal: the same explorer prompts, with the validator (parser-based control-flow alignment and LLM path-feasibility check) removed.
isolation_audit.other_changes: NoVal removes a verification stage. NoAbs removes a reasoning instruction from the prompt, not a supplied representation: the code shown to the LLM is the same and the LLM performs the abstraction itself.
isolation_audit.delta: Precision 78.43% (40TP/11FP) full vs 40.38% (21TP/31FP) NoAbs vs 40TP/38FP NoVal (51.28% computed from the totals; the paper does not state it)
isolation_audit.rationale: NoVal "removes the validation of the data-flow facts discovered by the explorer and also skips examining the bug reports," a verification-stage removal. NoAbs "skips the program abstraction, i.e., removing the second step in the prompt template," a change to the prompting procedure that leaves the supplied code representation unchanged. Neither arm isolates representation. The paper's NoVal text says FPs "increase to 31," but Table 6 and its +245.45% give 38.
isolation_audit.human_reason: Ablations remove a validator stage or a reasoning step of the prompt procedure; the code shown to the model is unchanged.

isolation_audit.comparison: Sec 5.6 (RQ6) Tables 7-8: MoCQ (DSL subset) vs DSL100 (complete DSL spec); DSL0 (no spec) appears only in Table 7
isolation_audit.model_config: Same in all arms: Claude 3.7 Sonnet, temperature 0.2, Joern backend, same feedback loop and "same iteration threshold" (20 iterations)
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: Table 7: 212 generation examples, query-generation pass rate; Table 8: test set, per-vulnerability-type F1 (average over 12 types)

isolation_audit.arm_a: Curated DSL subset (API signatures, types, functionality) in the query-generation prompt
isolation_audit.arm_b: DSL100: complete DSL specification (DSL0: no specification)
isolation_audit.other_changes: none between arms (symbolic validator, feedback, generalization and FP-elimination present in all); the varied context is the query-language specification, not the program representation, which is the same Joern CPG in every arm
isolation_audit.delta: Table 7 pass rate 77.4% (MoCQ) vs 50.0% (DSL100) vs 9.9% (DSL0); Table 8 average F1 0.51 vs 0.31 (DSL100). Text gives DSL100 pass rate as 49.1%, inconsistent with Table 7's 50.0%
isolation_audit.rationale: "We compare MoCQ with DSL subsetting against two variants: (1) DSL100 with a complete DSL specification (no subsetting) and (2) DSL0 with no specification" under the same model, loop and iteration threshold, and the subset arm is shorter, so MoCQ vs DSL100 meets R-strict. Caveat for the survey: this isolates grammar-spec context, not a code representation, so it should not be counted as evidence that program structure helps; DSL0 vs MoCQ alone would be R-unmatched-budget.

isolation_audit.comparison: Table 4 (Section 5.1): DeepSeek-R1 + CoT at API Level 3 (A3) vs. without API Level (w/o)
isolation_audit.model_config: DeepSeek-R1 with Chain-of-Thought prompt in both arms; temperature 0.1, max_tokens 512 (output)

isolation_audit.arm_b: Target function only ('No contextual information')

A1-A4 comparisons are cleaner against each other but are not reported as length-matched either.

isolation_audit.comparison: §4.1 RQ1, Table 1: LLM4PFA vs LLM4SA (and LLMDFA), NPD; also §4.4 Table 4: LLM4PFA vs NoContext / BatchSol
isolation_audit.model_config: GPT-4o-mini backbone, temperature 0, in all arms
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: SAFP-Bench-C (Linux kernel, OpenSSL, Libav); FPR_R (false-positive reduction recall), also Acc/FPR_P/Pre/Recall
isolation_audit.budget_control: Not reported
isolation_audit.arm_a: LLM4PFA: agent-driven iterative, self-planned context retrieval along the path + LLM-extracted path constraints solved iteratively with an SMT solver
isolation_audit.arm_b: LLM4SA: single prompt with the code snippet + bug report (public implementation); LLMDFA: dataflow summarization + Z3 path validation script synthesis
isolation_audit.other_changes: Analysis algorithm and pipeline differ: agent tool loop for context retrieval and SMT constraint solving (symbolic verification) in LLM4PFA vs a single prompt in LLM4SA. The §4.4 ablations remove the agent context-analysis loop (NoContext) or the iterative solving (BatchSol), both pipeline components
isolation_audit.delta: NPD FPR_R: LLM4SA 0.51 -> LLM4PFA 0.72; LLMDFA 0.35 -> 0.72; paper: 'FPR_R improvement of 41.1% - 105.7%' (relative). Ablation: '136.7% - 173.1% improvements in FPR_R' over NoContext/BatchSol (Total FPR_R 0.71 vs 0.26/0.30)
isolation_audit.rationale: Same model and dataset, but the arms differ in a full pipeline: an agent tool loop and SMT-based constraint solving vs LLM4SA's single 'code snippet and the bug report' prompt. The §4.4 variants also remove components ('NoContext performs symbolic range reasoning without iterative context analysis driven by the LLM agent'). No comparison in the paper varies only the representation.

isolation_audit.source_checked: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.11561v1 (no HTML version available; v1 is the only version)
isolation_audit.comparison: Table 1 / Sec 4.2: GPT-4o baseline (11-12-14) vs Short + CVE Hints + Manual (18-14-17). The cleaner within-template comparison is Short (13-13-13) vs Short + CVE Hints + Manual.
isolation_audit.model_config: GPT-4o in all arms, temperature 0.01, 3 generations per prompt

isolation_audit.budget_control: not controlled or reported. The Short prompt was designed for "minimizing token usage," but token counts are not given, and the added-context arms add CVE guidelines plus manual repository context on top of Short.
isolation_audit.arm_a: GPT-4o baseline: the original prompt from the prior study (parent class header, data members, vulnerable method). Cleaner alternative: Short, a condensed system prompt with refined code input.
isolation_audit.arm_b: Short + CVE Hints + Manual: Short prompt plus GPT-generated CVE-based repair guidelines plus "manually collected repository and issue-related information"
isolation_audit.other_changes: Against the GPT-4o baseline, the instruction template and code-input preparation also differ (Sec 3.2: added method headers, imports, pruned data members, new system prompt). Against Short there are no other changes; the paradigm stays zero-shot single prompt.
isolation_audit.delta: 18-14-17 vs 11-12-14 (baseline) and vs 13-13-13 (Short), successful repairs out of 42 per run; absolute counts, no pp or relative figure stated

The added-context arm appends CVE guidelines and "manually collected repository and issue-related information," and its length is not reported, so representation is confounded with context amount. The cited baseline arm also uses a different instruction template, so Short vs Short + CVE Hints + Manual is the cleaner comparison. Neither is R-strict. Short + Manual alone (9-13-10) scored below Short.

isolation_audit.comparison: Sec 5.2 (RQ2) Table 2: full vs w/o RAG, w/o AST, w/o PoV (record's headline is w/o RAG, -29 pp)
isolation_audit.model_config: Same in all arms: GPT-4o (temperature 0) for Reflector, Grader and Expert agents; OpenAI text-embedding-3-small; Qdrant, similarity threshold 0.35

isolation_audit.rationale: The cited headline arm removes the agentic retrieval stage, not just a representation ("w/o RAG, where only the target function ... is provided as context"). The closest representation arm, w/o AST ("AST-guided code segmentation is replaced with naive line-based chunking"), still acts through the retrieval loop with unreported context amounts, so it is at best R-unmatched-budget; no R-strict comparison exists.

isolation_audit.comparison: Section 5.7 (RQ3), Figure 10: full LTFix vs. LTFix-NT (no context trace)

isolation_audit.arm_b: Error report + error-propagation path, context trace omitted

isolation_audit.rationale: Same LLM and prompt, and only the context trace is removed ('omits the context trace in the prompts while maintaining all other components unchanged'), but the full arm is strictly longer and no per-arm token budget is reported. isolation_audit.comparison: Appendix C: LLMxCPG-D on CPG slices vs the same LLMxCPG-D on full code (slicing step bypassed)
isolation_audit.model_config: Same fine-tuned LLMxCPG-D (QwQ-32B-Preview + LoRA, reduced Yes/No classification head) in both arms; note LLMxCPG-D was fine-tuned on slices only (§3, 'fine-tuning dataset for classifying code slices')

isolation_audit.arm_b: Full function code

Caveats: (1) the record mislabels these as F1, but the paper reports accuracy; (2) LLMxCPG-D was fine-tuned on slices, so the train/test mismatch favours the slice arm and the gap is an upper bound on the representation effect.

isolation_audit.source_checked: https://arxiv.org/html/2508.13092 (latest; abs page lists v3, 21 Aug 2025)
isolation_audit.comparison: Table 2: LLM-only vs LLM+Knowledge vs VerilogLAVD, per backbone
isolation_audit.model_config: The same backbones (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3) are used across arms, 5 runs each, Pass@5. The LLM's role differs: judge in the baselines, rule generator in VerilogLAVD.
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: 77 Verilog designs (59 positive / 18 negative, 12 CWEs); precision/recall/F1
isolation_audit.budget_control: not reported
isolation_audit.arm_a: LLM+Knowledge: Verilog code, a brief CWE description, and detailed MITRE CWE information; the LLM judges directly
isolation_audit.arm_b: VerilogLAVD: the LLM generates VeriPG traversal rules, checked by a rule-validation tool with feedback, and a rule executor traverses the VeriPG graph (AST+CFG+DDG) to detect
isolation_audit.other_changes: Adds a symbolic rule executor (detection is done by graph traversal, not by the LLM) and a rule-validation feedback loop. The LLM's task changes from classification to rule generation.
isolation_audit.delta: F1 0.57 vs 0.25 (GPT-4o) and 0.50 vs 0.34 (DeepSeek-V3), absolute F1. Abstract and conclusion inconsistent: abstract F1 0.54 and gain 0.27 vs conclusion 0.25.
isolation_audit.rationale: The paper states that "LLMs are responsible for generating VeriPG traversal-based detection rules," which "avoids direct structural reasoning": a rule executor performs detection over the graph, and a validator feeds back during generation. The arms therefore differ by symbolic execution and verification components, not by the representation given to the same LLM judgment. There is no arm in which the LLM judges with the graph as input.

isolation_audit.arm_b: Task description + k randomly sampled in-context examples (code + labels) + test code

isolation_audit.comparison: RQ1 original code vs. L2 comment-deletion obfuscation
isolation_audit.model_config: same evaluated model and fixed temperature 10^-5; same dataset and 1–4 type-detection metric
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: Smart-bugs, PrimeVul, ReposVul_cpp, ReposVul_py; detection success rate (type evaluation: score 3/4 positive) and downgrade/upgrade counts ('attack success rate'); RQ3 uses the relaxed existence evaluation
isolation_audit.budget_control: No explicit token-budget control; L2 deletes comments/docstrings, so its supplied code is not longer than the original.
isolation_audit.arm_a: unobfuscated source code
isolation_audit.arm_b: L2 obfuscated source code with comments/docstrings deleted
isolation_audit.other_changes: None at detection time; only the code representation differs.
isolation_audit.delta: Virtualization 'attack success rate of up to approximately 80% on the C/C++ datasets'; mixed-language 'around 75%' (Finding #2). RQ3 existence evaluation: QWEN-14B PrimeVul 'jumps from 0.39 on the original code to 0.80 after applying L1 obfuscation'
isolation_audit.rationale: Same model and prompt, and only the code text differs ('For each obfuscated sample, we compared the model's detection results against its unobfuscated counterpart'). Input length is not controlled or reported, and virtualization/mixed-language transforms add code, so the conservative rule applies. This is also a surface-form perturbation, not a structured representation, so it does not test structure vs text. The 0.39->0.80 example uses the relaxed existence criterion, under which 'obfuscation rarely reduces detection success'.
isolation_audit.human_reason: Original vs comment-deleted code, same model and prompt, shorter obfuscated arm. Flagged: varies surface form, not program structure.

isolation_audit.comparison: RQ3 ablation, Table IV (CodeQL rulesets R1-R7). The cited RQ1 comparison is CodeQL default vs SemTaint.
isolation_audit.model_config: Detection is done by CodeQL in every arm. LLM agents (GPT-5 for Source/Sink and Flow Summary, GPT-5-mini for CallGraph) only produce specifications. The record's "GPT-4 vs GPT-4-mini" is incorrect.
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: Known Vulnerability Dataset, 162 test instances; recall and first-detecting ruleset
isolation_audit.budget_control: not applicable (the varied input feeds a static analyzer, not an LLM prompt)

isolation_audit.arm_b: R4/R6: custom or combined sources/sinks with the LLM-repaired (enhanced) call graph. R1: CodeQL defaults with no LLM.

isolation_audit.rationale: The paper says "the resulting taint specification is then provided to a SAST tool, which performs vulnerability analysis." RQ3 therefore adds or removes LLM-generated pipeline components (call-graph repair) inside CodeQL, not the representation an LLM reasons over. RQ1 compares against a non-LLM tool and is not isolated. The combined-dataset split (73.0/27.0) should not be mixed with the testing-only split (76.4/23.6).

isolation_audit.comparison: Table 10 (Section 4.5): Full VulnAgent-R2 vs. w/o graph context optimizer
isolation_audit.model_config: Agents use Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, temperature 0.2, in both arms; rest of the multi-agent pipeline (CER, Sceptic, VPS, memory, calibration, scheduler) retained

isolation_audit.arm_b: Context without the graph optimizer (the replacement selection procedure is not described)

The full arm also uses more tokens (9,410 vs 7,810). The other Table 10 rows (w/o CER, Sceptic, VPS) are verification/agent components and cannot serve as representation ablations.

isolation_audit.arm_b: One stage removed: symbolic extractor (rule-based static analysis), neuro extractor (LLM), symbolic reasoner, or neuro reasoner (LLM)

isolation_audit.dataset_metric: v1: 28 CVEs from ReposVul (CWE-200, CWE-284); v2: 35 CVEs; number of CVEs detected (true positives)
isolation_audit.budget_control: Not controlled; removing either context source shortens the prompt (v2 cost section: "both the function-level grounding and the repository-level bundle dominate its prompt size")
isolation_audit.arm_a: Function + local augmentation bundle (depth-one callee signatures/bodies, macros, constants, typedefs) + repository-level context bundle
isolation_audit.arm_b: -Local: function + repository bundle only; -Repo: function + local augmentation only
isolation_audit.other_changes: -Local: none beyond prompt content. -Repo: also removes an upstream pipeline stage, the bundle is "produced by a repository-level LLM agent" run once per repository
isolation_audit.delta: v1 Table IV: Opus 4.7 15 -> 9 (-Local) and 9 (-Repo); GPT-5.4 12 -> 8 and 7 detections (of 28). v2 Table 4: Opus 20 -> 13 and 11; GPT-5.4 14 -> 9 and 8 (of 35)
isolation_audit.rationale: Same backbone and data, and -Local only withholds the depth-one program context from the prompt, but the full arm is substantially longer with no budget control, so the comparison measures added context rather than representation alone. The -Repo arm additionally removes an LLM-agent summarization stage and is closer to a component ablation. The record's numbers match v1; v2 enlarges the set to 35 CVEs with different counts.

isolation_audit.comparison: Table IV (RQ1, Section V-C): LeanGuard vs. Pure LLM baseline, DeepSeek-V4-Pro backend
isolation_audit.model_config: DeepSeek-V4-Pro at temperature 0 for all neural components in both arms; CWE-120/416/476 report best of three runs, CWE-125/415 single runs
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: Merged PrimeVul + ReposVul + R2Vul, 5 CWE classes; F1 (also accuracy, precision, recall)
isolation_audit.budget_control: not controlled; the pipelines differ in number and type of LLM calls (fact editing, optional refinement) vs a single verdict call
isolation_audit.arm_a: Six-stage pipeline: AST candidate extraction, LLM constrained fact-editing filter, deterministic reconciliation and auto-pairing, Lean 4 kernel-checked verification, one-shot neuro-symbolic refinement, evidence-aware adjudication
isolation_audit.arm_b: LLM 'reads the function and emits a verdict directly'
isolation_audit.other_changes: Symbolic verification stage (Lean 4), deterministic auto-pairing, refinement, and adjudication added. The LLM's task also changes from verdict to fact editor
isolation_audit.delta: CWE-416 F1 0.3652 -> 0.5000 (+0.1348 absolute); CWE-415 F1 0.4324 -> 0.6237 (+0.1913 absolute) (Table IV, Pure LLM rows)
isolation_audit.rationale: The backend is held fixed ('which isolates the effect of the pipeline from differences in the underlying model'), but the arms differ by a Lean 4 symbolic verifier, auto-pairing and adjudication, and the LLM's role changes from decision maker to 'fact editor'. This is a same-model pipeline ablation, not a representation one. The internal 'w/o AST' ablation (Table V) also changes the LLM's task, so no R-strict comparison exists.

isolation_audit.comparison: §V RQ2, Table II: full AgenticRepair vs w/o Code-Structure / w/o Program-Execution / w/o Commit-History Context (strict mode)
isolation_audit.model_config: gpt-5.2-2025-12-11, medium reasoning effort, temperature 1.0; analysis subagents max 20 steps, repair subagent max 75 steps; same multi-agent scaffold
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: SEC-Bench 200 CVE-sourced instances; repair success rate (strict mode)
isolation_audit.budget_control: Step caps only (20/75 steps); context/token budget not controlled or reported
isolation_audit.arm_a: Full: three ReAct context-engineering subagents (code-structure via CodeQL etc., runtime via GDB/Valgrind, commit history) produce partial contexts synthesized into the repair subagent's episodic memory
isolation_audit.arm_b: One facet removed: the corresponding context subagent and its partial context are absent
isolation_audit.other_changes: Removing a facet removes an entire tool-using ReAct subagent (its tool loop and tools, e.g. CodeQL) and shortens the context; single run at temperature 1.0
isolation_audit.delta: Strict success 75.0% (150) -> 73.5% (147) w/o code-structure (-1.5 pp), 74.5% (149) w/o execution (-0.5 pp), 73.0% (146) w/o commit-history (-2.0 pp) (Table II)
isolation_audit.rationale: Each facet is produced by a separate ReAct subagent that 'selects and invokes domain-specific tools to gather its facet of information', so the ablation removes an agent tool-loop component, not only a representation. The deltas (1-4 of 200 instances, single run at temperature 1.0) are within run-to-run noise. Note: the record's structure_gain cites 73.0-74.5% for the facet ablations, but the code-structure arm is 73.5%.

isolation_audit.comparison: Table 3 node ablation: full CLEAR vs No VCKG (Agent Only), and vs No Fix Intent, on PrimeVul
isolation_audit.model_config: gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0.0, for "baselines and ablation variants"; same multi-agent architecture
isolation_audit.dataset_metric: PrimeVul; Pairwise-Correct (P-C)
isolation_audit.budget_control: not reported for the ablation (Top-k=5 and 2-hop windowing are mentioned only for retrieval and graph construction)
isolation_audit.arm_a: Full CLEAR: the Collector Agent retrieves Top-5 similar historical nodes from the VCKG (built from the training split), expands them along graph edges, and LLM-filters them; the Claim and other agents use these contexts
isolation_audit.arm_b: No VCKG (Agent Only): the multi-agent pipeline without the knowledge graph. The paper does not describe what agents receive instead.
isolation_audit.other_changes: Removing the VCKG removes the Collector's similarity-retrieval stage, graph expansion, and LLM filtering/retry step, a retrieval component and not just the shown context. Node-type ablations change what retrieval can return.
isolation_audit.delta: P-C 19.17 (full) vs 8.08 (No VCKG) vs 14.32 (No Fix Intent); absolute P-C
isolation_audit.rationale: The VCKG enters through a retrieval stage in which the Collector "interacts with the global VCKG to perform a semantic similarity comparison, retrieving the Top-5 most similar historical EP nodes," followed by graph expansion and LLM filtering. No VCKG removes that stage, and the paper does not say what replaces it. Context length is not reported for any arm, so even the node-type ablations are not R-strict.
isolation_audit.human_reason: Removing the knowledge graph also removes the similarity-retrieval stage, graph expansion and an LLM filter/retry step.

isolation_records.structure_gain: Removing the AC Context Graph (ACG, built from interprocedural slicing+PDG+call graph) drops success from 94.92% to 89.83% (-5.09pp) on the same GPT-4 model with RBAC taxonomy and validator held constant (§VII-C Table IV)
isolation_records.confound_note: Headline comparison (vanilla GPT-4 vs full ACFix) varies representation (ACG), retrieved knowledge (RBAC taxonomy), and agent loop (validator) simultaneously; a component-wise ablation (Table IV) isolates ACG's contribution alone by holding RBAC+validator+model fixed

isolation_records.structure_gain: eCPG-based slicing (vs full-file raw context, LLM4FPM-noslice) improves accuracy by +3.02pp and F1 by +1.73pp on the same Qwen2.5-32B model (Table III); the raw-file variant also fails outright on 40 cases due to context-window overflow.
isolation_records.confound_note: RQ3 ablation (Table III) isolates representation by holding the LLM fixed while toggling eCPG-slicing and FARF; the RQ1 comparison to prior SOTA LLM4SA confounds representation with differing prompting strategy and self-consistency voting.

isolation_records.structure_gain: Providing a subset DSL grammar (MoCQ) instead of no specification raises query-generation pass rate from 9.9% (DSL0) to 77.4%, and F1 from 0.31 (DSL100, full grammar) to 0.51 (MoCQ), same LLM loop (Tables 7-8).
isolation_records.confound_note: The DSL0/DSL100/MoCQ ablation varies only the amount/form of structured grammar given to the same iterative LLM loop -- a clean representation-only ablation; the SOTA comparison (Table 4, vs Pure LLM/GRACE/KNighter/IRIS) also changes analysis architecture entirely.

isolation_records.structure_gain: Appendix C same-model slicing ablation: slice-based vs full-code F1 0.8146 vs 0.6762 (FormAI), 0.7250 vs 0.4875 (PrimeVul), 0.6020 vs 0.5078 (SVEN) — the extractor's claim that these were 'not detailed' was wrong.
isolation_records.confound_note: Baselines (ReGVD, VulBERTA, VulSim) differ from LLMxCPG in both representation (embeddings/graphs vs CPG-derived slice) and model architecture (GNN/BERT vs fine-tuned LLM) simultaneously; not a same-architecture ablation

isolation_records.structure_gain: Equal-shot comparison: 10-shot retrieval-augmented vs random examples, F1 71.43% vs 65.69% (+5.74pp), same Gemini-1.5-Flash (Sec. V-B). The zero-shot vs 20-shot pair (36.35% -> 74.05%) also changes the amount of context.
isolation_records.confound_note: Few-shot arms (random vs retrieval-augmented vs retrieval-based labeling) hold the base model fixed and vary only the example-selection mechanism -- a clean representation-only ablation; the separate fine-tuned CodeBERT/Gemini comparisons change both model and training paradigm.

isolation_records.structure_gain: Central ablation compares raw code text vs. its obfuscated (layout/data-flow/control-flow-transformed) counterpart, same LLM/prompt: virtualization obfuscation degrades detection with up to ~80% attack success rate on C/C++ (Finding #2); conversely some layout obfuscations (e.g., L1) 'upgrade' detection by removing misleading surface cues, e.g. QWEN-14B on PrimeVul jumps from 0.39 to 0.80 success after L1 (Section 4.2.3).
isolation_records.confound_note: Table 6's original-vs-obfuscated comparison holds the LLM, prompt template, and underlying ground-truth vulnerability fixed and varies only the raw-text obfuscation transformation -- a clean representation-only ablation, though 'representation' here means raw-text surface form (layout/data-flow/control-flow perturbation) rather than a structured alternative such as AST or CFG.

isolation_records.structure_gain: AST+PDG reaches 83.2% curated accuracy vs. 53.5% for raw source alone (+29.7pp), with model (qwen3.6-plus), temperature, prompting/checklist structure, and 50,000-character budget held fixed across all ten representation variants (§4.2, §5.2 Table 6)
isolation_records.confound_note: Model, temperature, prompting structure, and character budget are held constant across representation variants; program representation is the sole varied factor (§4.2) -- this is the study's central, deliberately isolated ablation
